body:
Why electric current produces heat

When electric current passes through a conductor having resistance, electrical energy may be converted into heat. This is called the heating effect of electric current.

In a purely resistive circuit, the electrical energy delivered to the resistor appears as heat. In other appliances, electrical energy may also be converted into useful mechanical energy, light or sound.

Joule's law of heating

For a resistor of resistance \(R\), carrying a steady current \(I\) for a time \(t\), the heat produced is:

\(H=I^2Rt\)

This is known as Joule's law of heating. The heat is measured in joules (J) when current, resistance and time are expressed in SI units.

The law gives 3 important relationships:

  • For fixed resistance and time, heat is proportional to the square of the current.
  • For fixed current and time, heat is directly proportional to resistance.
  • For fixed current and resistance, heat is directly proportional to time.

Thus, if current is doubled while resistance and time remain unchanged, the heat produced becomes 4 times as much.

Calculating heat

A current of 2 A passes through a 5 Ω resistor for 60 seconds. The heat generated is:

\(H=I^2Rt=2^2\times5\times60=1200\ \mathrm{J}\).

The importance of what remains constant

For an ohmic resistor, Ohm's law allows Joule's heating formula to be written in other forms:

\(H=VIt=\frac{V^2t}{R}\)

These forms explain an important distinction. When current is fixed, increasing resistance increases heating. When potential difference is fixed, decreasing resistance increases heating in an ideal ohmic resistor.

Consequently, the statement that a greater resistance always produces more heat is incomplete. The result depends on whether current or voltage is held constant.

Heating elements

Electric irons, kettles, ovens, toasters and room heaters use the heating effect deliberately. Their heating elements are commonly made from alloys such as nichrome.

Nichrome is suitable because it has relatively high resistivity, withstands high operating temperatures and resists rapid oxidation during normal use. The conductor is selected to provide the desired heating when connected to its rated supply.

Incandescent bulbs and LED lamps

An incandescent bulb produces light by heating a thin tungsten filament to a very high temperature. Tungsten is used because of its high melting point. However, much of the electrical energy supplied to an incandescent filament is emitted as heat rather than useful visible light.

An LED lamp produces light by a different process in a semiconductor. It does not need a filament heated until it glows. For a comparable useful light output, an LED lamp generally consumes less electrical power than an incandescent lamp.

Therefore, a lamp's brightness and its wattage should not be treated as identical quantities. Wattage indicates the rate of electrical energy consumption; light output depends on the technology and efficiency of the lamp.

When heating becomes dangerous

In ordinary connecting wires, excessive heating is undesirable. A current greater than the wire or appliance can safely carry may overheat insulation and create a fire hazard.

The heating effect also explains how a traditional electric fuse operates. A fuse contains a conductor designed to melt when excessive current flows for a sufficient time. Once it melts, the circuit opens and current stops. The detailed roles of fuses, circuit breakers and earthing in household protection are considered separately.

Prelims focus

  • Joule's law of heating is \(H=I^2Rt\).
  • At constant resistance and time, doubling current produces 4 times the heat.
  • At constant voltage and time, an ohmic resistor produces heat according to \(H=V^2t/R\).
  • Nichrome is commonly used for electrical heating elements.
  • Tungsten is used in incandescent bulb filaments because of its high melting point.
  • Trap: A greater resistance does not always mean more heat; the condition of fixed current or fixed voltage matters.

[NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 11, “Electricity,” printed pp. 188–191, sections 11.7–11.7.1; NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 14, “Electric Current and its Effects,” printed pp. 163–167.]

pictures.caption: Electric irons and kettles use electrical energy to produce heat.

title: Heating Effect of Electric Current and Electrical Heating Devices

body:
Power is the rate of energy use

Electrical appliances do not all consume electrical energy at the same rate. A small lamp generally requires less power than an electric heater. The quantity that expresses the rate of electrical energy conversion is electric power.

Electric power is the rate at which electrical energy is transferred or converted.

\(P=\frac{W}{t}=VI\)

Here, \(P\) is power, \(W\) is transferred energy, \(t\) is time, \(V\) is potential difference and \(I\) is current.

The SI unit of power is the watt (W). A device consumes 1 W when it converts 1 joule of energy every second.

\(1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J/s}=1\ \mathrm{V}\times1\ \mathrm{A}\)

A larger unit is the kilowatt:

\(1\ \mathrm{kW}=1000\ \mathrm{W}\)

Power formulas for resistors

Combining \(P=VI\) with Ohm's law gives 2 additional formulas for an ohmic resistor:

\(P=I^2R\)

\(P=\frac{V^2}{R}\)

All 3 forms are useful, but the known quantities determine which is most convenient.

  • Use \(P=VI\) when voltage and current are known.
  • Use \(P=I^2R\) when current and resistance are known.
  • Use \(P=V^2/R\) when voltage and resistance are known.

For example, an ohmic appliance operating at 12 V and drawing 2 A consumes power at a rate of \(P=12\times2=24\ \mathrm{W}\).

Electrical energy depends on power and time

Power and energy must not be confused. Power tells us how quickly energy is used. Energy tells us how much is used over a period of time.

For constant power:

\(E=Pt\)

The SI unit of energy is the joule. In electricity billing, a much larger unit is convenient: the kilowatt-hour (kWh).

One kilowatt-hour is the energy consumed by a device operating at a power of 1 kW for 1 hour.

\(1\ \mathrm{kWh}=1000\ \mathrm{W}\times3600\ \mathrm{s}\)

\(1\ \mathrm{kWh}=3.6\times10^6\ \mathrm{J}\)

In everyday electricity billing, 1 unit of electrical energy means 1 kWh. It is a unit of energy, not power.

Energy used by an electric heater

A 1000 W heater operates at its rated power for 2 hours. Since 1000 W equals 1 kW, the energy consumed is:

\(E=1\ \mathrm{kW}\times2\ \mathrm{h}=2\ \mathrm{kWh}\).

In joules, this is \(2\times3.6\times10^6=7.2\times10^6\ \mathrm{J}\).

Why operating time matters

A low-power appliance used for many hours can consume as much energy as a high-power appliance used briefly. For example, a 100 W device operating for 10 hours uses 1 kWh. A 1000 W device operating for 1 hour also uses 1 kWh.

A 10 W LED lamp used for 5 hours per day over 30 days consumes:

\(E=\frac{10\times5\times30}{1000}=1.5\ \mathrm{kWh}\).

The numerical result assumes that the lamp consumes 10 W whenever it operates. Actual consumption can differ when an appliance operates at changing power levels.

Understanding an appliance's power rating

An appliance marked 1000 W is rated to consume power at that rate under its specified operating conditions. It does not necessarily consume 1000 W continuously in every mode or situation.

For a simple resistive appliance, changing the applied voltage changes its power consumption. A rated voltage should not be ignored when comparing appliances or using power formulas.

Watt measures power. Kilowatt-hour measures energy. Electricity consumption depends on both the appliance's power and the duration of use.

Prelims focus

  • Electric power is \(P=VI\).
  • For an ohmic resistor, \(P=I^2R=V^2/R\).
  • The SI unit of power is watt; the SI unit of energy is joule.
  • 1 kW equals 1000 W.
  • 1 kWh equals \(3.6\times10^6\) J.
  • Trap: A kilowatt-hour is a unit of energy, not a unit of power.

[NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 11, “Electricity,” printed pp. 188–192, sections 11.7–11.8.]

pictures.alt: Equal shaded areas show that 100 W for 10 h and 1000 W for 1 h both consume 1000 Wh, or 1 kWh.
pictures.caption: Different combinations of power and operating time can consume the same electrical energy.

title: Electric Power, Electrical Energy and Electricity Consumption

body:
What makes a material magnetic?

A magnet can attract certain materials without touching them. Iron, nickel and cobalt are familiar magnetic materials. Ordinary materials such as wood, rubber and plastic are not strongly attracted to a bar magnet.

Permanent magnets are manufactured in several shapes, including bar, horseshoe and ring magnets. Their shapes differ, but the basic behaviour of their magnetic poles remains the same.

The 2 poles of a magnet

Every ordinary magnet has a north pole and a south pole. In a bar magnet, the magnetic effect is especially strong near its ends, where the poles are located.

When 2 magnets are brought near each other:

  • North pole facing north pole: repulsion.
  • South pole facing south pole: repulsion.
  • North pole facing south pole: attraction.

A magnet can also attract an unmagnetised iron object. Therefore, attraction alone does not establish that an unknown object is a magnet. Repulsion between 2 suitably oriented objects is a more decisive indication that both are magnetised.

Magnetic poles occur in pairs. Breaking a bar magnet into smaller pieces does not isolate a single north pole or a single south pole. Each resulting piece has its own north and south poles.

Magnetic compass

A compass contains a small magnetised needle that can rotate freely. Away from strong nearby magnetic disturbances, it approximately aligns itself along the north-south direction because Earth behaves like a large magnet.

The end of the needle that seeks the north direction is called its north-seeking pole. A compass can therefore be used to identify directions and to study the direction of magnetic fields near magnets and current-carrying conductors.

Nearby magnets, iron objects and electric currents can disturb the compass reading. The needle indicates the direction of the resultant magnetic field at its location rather than always pointing towards geographic north.

What is a magnetic field?

A magnetic field is the region around a magnet or current-carrying conductor in which magnetic effects can be detected.

Magnetic field lines are an imaginary representation of the direction and relative strength of a magnetic field. They help visualise a field that cannot be seen directly.

Direction of magnetic field lines

Outside a bar magnet, magnetic field lines are conventionally represented as emerging from the north pole and entering the south pole. Inside the magnet, they continue from the south pole towards the north pole.

Thus, complete magnetic field lines form closed curves. They do not simply stop at the ends of the magnet.

Properties of magnetic field lines

  • Direction: At a point, the magnetic field direction is the direction in which the north end of a small compass needle points.
  • Relative strength: The field is represented as stronger where field lines are drawn closer together.
  • Closed paths: Field lines form continuous closed curves.
  • No intersections: Two field lines cannot cross, because a magnetic field cannot have 2 different directions at the same point.

Field lines are a way of representing the field; they are not physical threads or paths along which iron filings must travel. Iron filings tend to align along the local magnetic field, making its pattern visible.

Permanent magnets and electromagnets

A permanent magnet retains significant magnetism without requiring a continuous electric current. An electromagnet produces magnetism through current flowing in a coil, often strengthened by an iron core. Its magnetic effect can be controlled by switching the current on or off.

This distinction becomes useful when studying electric bells, magnetic cranes and motors.

Prelims focus

  • Iron, nickel and cobalt are familiar magnetic materials.
  • Like magnetic poles repel; unlike poles attract.
  • Magnetic poles remain paired even when a magnet is cut into pieces.
  • Outside a bar magnet, magnetic field lines run from north pole to south pole.
  • Magnetic field lines form closed curves and do not intersect.
  • Trap: A stronger magnetic field is represented by more closely spaced field lines, not by intersecting field lines.

[NCERT, Science, Class 6, Curiosity, Chapter 4, “Exploring Magnets,” printed pp. 61–69; NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 12, “Magnetic Effects of Electric Current,” printed pp. 195–197, section 12.1.]

pictures.caption: Magnetic field lines form closed curves and are more crowded near the poles.

title: Magnets, Magnetic Poles and Magnetic Field Lines

body:
The connection between electricity and magnetism

Electricity and magnetism are closely related. A wire carrying electric current produces a magnetic field around it. This effect was demonstrated by Hans Christian Oersted in 1820, when he observed that current flowing through a nearby wire deflected a compass needle.

The deflection shows that the magnetic field produced by the current interacts with the compass needle. When the direction of current is reversed, the direction of the magnetic field around the wire also reverses.

Field around a straight current-carrying conductor

For a long straight conductor, magnetic field lines form concentric circles centred on the wire. The circles lie in planes perpendicular to the wire.

At a fixed distance from the wire, the field becomes stronger when the current increases. For the same current, the field becomes weaker farther from the wire.

Right-hand thumb rule

The direction of the magnetic field around a straight current-carrying conductor is obtained using the right-hand thumb rule.

Imagine holding the conductor in your right hand so that your thumb points along the direction of conventional current. Your curled fingers then indicate the direction of the circular magnetic field lines.

For a wire carrying current towards the observer, the field circles anticlockwise as viewed by that observer. For current directed away from the observer, the field circles clockwise.

The right-hand thumb rule tells the direction of the magnetic field around a current. It is different from Fleming's left-hand rule, which tells the direction of force on a current-carrying conductor.

Magnetic field of a circular current-carrying loop

When a straight conductor is bent into a circular loop, current in each part of the loop produces a magnetic field. Near the centre, the fields from different parts of the loop combine in the same general direction.

Looking directly at one face of a circular loop:

  • Anticlockwise conventional current produces a magnetic field through the centre directed towards the observer. That face behaves like a north-pole face.
  • Clockwise conventional current produces a magnetic field through the centre directed away from the observer. That face behaves like a south-pole face.

If a coil has more turns carrying current in the same direction, their magnetic effects reinforce one another. This allows a coil to produce a stronger field than a single turn under otherwise comparable conditions.

Solenoid and its magnetic field

A solenoid is a long coil made of many closely wound turns of insulated conducting wire. When current passes through it, the magnetic field resembles the field of a bar magnet.

One end of the solenoid behaves like a north pole and the other like a south pole. Inside a sufficiently long current-carrying solenoid, away from its ends, field lines are approximately straight, parallel and equally spaced. This represents a nearly uniform magnetic field.

The polarity of a solenoid can be reversed by reversing the direction of current. Its magnetic field becomes stronger when the current increases, other conditions remaining the same.

Why this matters

A straight wire, a circular loop and a solenoid all demonstrate the same basic principle: electric current produces a magnetic field. The shape of the current-carrying conductor determines the pattern of that field.

Prelims focus

  • Oersted demonstrated the magnetic effect of electric current in 1820.
  • The magnetic field around a straight current-carrying wire consists of concentric circles.
  • The right-hand thumb rule gives the direction of that field.
  • Reversing the current reverses the magnetic-field direction.
  • A current-carrying solenoid behaves like a bar magnet.
  • Trap: A solenoid's field is approximately uniform inside a sufficiently long coil, not necessarily everywhere outside it.

[NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 12, “Magnetic Effects of Electric Current,” printed pp. 195 and 198–201, sections 12.2.1–12.2.4.]

pictures.caption: The right-hand thumb rule relates current direction to the circular magnetic field.
